{{Short description|Mathematical framework for identifying causal effects}}
{{Italic title|string=Do}}

'''''Do''-calculus''' is a set of mathematical rules devised by [[Judea Pearl]] in 1995 to determine whether [[causality|causal effects]] can be identified from observational data under specific assumptions encoded in a [[causal graph]]. It provides a systematic method for transforming expressions involving the ''do''-operator (representing interventions) into expressions involving only observable probabilities, enabling the identification of causal relationships.

== Definition and purpose ==
{{Improve|reason=Formula missing|date=December 2025}}
Causal queries involving interventions (e.g., <math> P(y \mid \mathrm{do}(x)) </math>) are considered ''[[identifiable]]'' if they can be expressed using observational data alone, independent of unmeasured parameters. The ''do''-calculus achieves this by leveraging graphical criteria from [[directed acyclic graphs]] (DAGs) to remove ''do''-operators through algebraic manipulations.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last1=Pearl |first1=Judea |author-link=Judea Pearl |url={{google books |plainurl=y |id=9H0dDQAAQBAJ}} |title=The Book of Why: The New Science of Cause and Effect |last2=Mackenzie |first2=Dana |date=2018-05-15 |publisher=Basic Books |isbn=9780465097616 |language=en}}</ref>

== The three rules of ''Do''-calculus ==
The rules<ref>{{Cite web |title=Causal Models > Supplement 2. The do-calculus (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy) |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/causal-models/do-calculus.html#:~:text=The%20do-calculus%20is%20an,certain%20substitutions%20may%20be%20made. |access-date=2025-04-15 |website=plato.stanford.edu |language=en}}</ref> apply to a causal graph <math>\mathcal{G}</math> and assume the [[Markov condition]] holds:

=== Rule 1: Insertion/deletion of observations ===
:<math>
P(y \mid \mathrm{do}(x), z, w) = P(y \mid \mathrm{do}(x), w) \quad \text{if } Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z \mid X, W \text{ in } \mathcal{G}_{\overline{X}}
</math>

This rule allows the removal of irrelevant observations (<math>Z</math>) if they are ''d''-separated from <math>Y</math> given <math>X</math> and <math>W</math> in the graph where incoming edges to <math>X</math> are removed.

=== Rule 2: Action/observation exchange ===
:<math>
P(y \mid \mathrm{do}(x), \mathrm{do}(z), w) = P(y \mid \mathrm{do}(x), z, w) \quad \text{if } Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z \mid X, W \text{ in } \mathcal{G}_{\overline{X}\, \underline{Z}}
</math>

This rule permits replacing an intervention (<math>\mathrm{do}(z)</math>) with an observation (<math>z</math>) if <math>Y</math> and <math>Z</math> are ''d''-separated in the graph where outgoing edges from <math>Z</math> and incoming edges to <math>X</math> are removed.

=== Rule 3: Insertion/deletion of interventions ===
:<math>
P(y \mid \mathrm{do}(x), \mathrm{do}(z), w) = P(y \mid \mathrm{do}(x), w) \quad \text{if } Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z \mid X, W \text{ in } \mathcal{G}_{\overline{X}\, \overline{Z(W)}}
</math>

This rule removes irrelevant interventions (<math>\mathrm{do}(z)</math>) if <math>Y</math> and <math>Z</math> are ''d''-separated in a graph modified to block paths through <math>Z</math>.

== Applications ==
''Do''-calculus can be applied to various domains within [[causal inference]] such as [[Mediation (statistics)|mediation analysis]] in decomposing direct and indirect effects.<ref name="pearl2012">{{Cite journal |last=Pearl |first=Judea |title=The Do-Calculus Revisited |journal=Journal of Causal Inference |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=37–45 |year=2012 |url=https://ftp.cs.ucla.edu/pub/stat_ser/r402.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Malinsky |first=Daniel |title=A Potential Outcomes Calculus for Identifying Conditional Path-Specific Effects |journal=Proceedings of Machine Learning Research |volume=89 |pages=3080–3088 |year=2019 |url=http://proceedings.mlr.press/v89/malinsky19b/malinsky19b.pdf}}</ref> It can be used for meta-synthesis to combine the results from heterogeneous studies.<ref name="pearl2012" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bareinboim |first=Elias |title=Causal Inference and Data Fusion in Econometrics |url=https://causalai.net/r51.pdf |journal=The Econometrics Journal |access-date=2025-04-15}}</ref>

== Completeness ==
The ''do''-calculus is considered [[Completeness (logic)|complete]]: if repeated application of the rules cannot eliminate the ''do''-operator, the causal effect is not identifiable. This result was formalized in 2006 by Huang, Valtorta, Shpitser, and Pearl.<ref name="pearl2012">{{Cite journal |last=Pearl |first=Judea |title=The Do-Calculus Revisited |journal=Journal of Causal Inference |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=37–45 |year=2012 |url=https://ftp.cs.ucla.edu/pub/stat_ser/r402.pdf}}</ref>

== Criticism ==

Critics have pointed out that other frameworks, such as [[structural equation modeling]] (SEM) or [[Bayesian network|Bayesian networks]], may offer more intuitive approaches to causal inference for certain applications. These methods often emphasize parameter estimation rather than identifiability, which can be more relevant for applied research.<ref name="bottou">{{Cite journal |last=Bottou |first=Léon |title=Counterfactual Reasoning and Learning Systems: The Example of Computational Advertising |journal=Journal of Machine Learning Research |volume=14 |pages=3207–3260 |year=2013 |url=https://jmlr.org/papers/volume14/bottou13a/bottou13a.pdf}}</ref>
